Nala carries Varuṇa's marriage proposal to Damayantī.
Varuṇa assumes Nala's form while competing for Damayantī.
Varuṇa accepts Damayantī's choice and grants Nala command or availability of water.
Kali possesses Nala after a ritual lapse and causes his ruin and abandonment.
Damayantī's curse and Karkoṭaka's poison torment Kali until he leaves Nala.
Kali promises not to harm those who recite Nala's story.
Vāyu testifies from the sky that Damayantī remained faithful.
Bali is Prahlāda’s grandson through Virocana.
Prahlāda teaches Bali that anger and forgiveness must suit circumstances.
Prahlāda consoles Bali, supports him, and accompanies him to Sutala.
Narasiṃha kills Hiraṇyakaśipu and ends Prahlāda’s persecution.
Narasiṃha touches Prahlāda, receives his hymn, and installs him as ruler.
Prahlāda hears Nārada’s devotional teaching while still in Kayādhu’s womb.
Indra captures Prahlāda’s pregnant mother but releases her after Nārada intervenes.
Disguised as a brahmin, Indra requests and receives Prahlāda’s śīla.
Brahmā addresses Narasiṃha and Prahlāda after the pillar theophany.
Ajagara teaches Prahlāda contentment, impermanence, and freedom from desire.
Prahlāda attempts and fails to lift Skanda’s spear.
Prahlāda advises his Daitya kinsman against aggression, but Andhaka disregards him.
Brahmā decrees that Aśvapati will receive a daughter; no direct meeting occurs.
Nārada hears Sāvitrī’s choice, predicts Satyavān’s death, and approves her resolve.
Sītā names Sāvitrī as her model for faithfully following her husband.
Rāma hears Sītā compare herself to Sāvitrī devoted to Satyavān.
Indra sends Menakā to disrupt Viśvāmitra, indirectly causing Śakuntalā’s conception.
Indra’s summons indirectly brings Duṣyanta toward his reunion with Śakuntalā.
Kāma assists Menakā’s seduction of Viśvāmitra, indirectly enabling Śakuntalā’s birth.
Kāma metaphorically afflicts Śakuntalā and Duṣyanta with love.
Vāyu exposes Menakā’s garment during the stratagem preceding Śakuntalā’s conception.
Aditi receives Śakuntalā, Duṣyanta, and their son at Marīca’s hermitage.
Sūrya is Sugrīva’s divine father and generator.

god_relations.myth: Sugrīva’s final return to the Sun
god_relations.note: Sugrīva enters the Sarayū and returns into the solar orb.
Agni witnesses the solemn compact between Sugrīva and Rāma.
Sugrīva promises help finding Sītā; Rāma promises to remove Vāli.
Rāma kills Vāli and restores Sugrīva to Kiṣkindhā’s throne.

god_relations.myth: Search for Sītā and Laṅkā war
god_relations.note: Sugrīva mobilizes his coalition, commands searches, and fights in Rāma’s campaign.
Rāma condemns Sugrīva’s delayed fulfillment and later rebukes his reckless attack on Rāvaṇa.

god_relations.myth: Search for Sītā and Laṅkā war
god_relations.note: Sugrīva preserves Sītā’s dropped ornaments and mobilizes forces contributing to her rescue.
Hanumān serves as Sugrīva’s minister, treaty broker, counselor, emissary, and commander.

god_relations.myth: Sampāti directs the southern search party
god_relations.note: Sampāti tells Sugrīva’s agents that Sītā is in Laṅkā, without meeting Sugrīva.
Sugrīva impulsively attacks and wrestles Rāvaṇa before escaping to Rāma.
Sugrīva sees Rāvaṇa carrying Sītā away and later produces her dropped ornaments.

god_relations.myth: Divine generation of the rival brothers
god_relations.note: Indra fathers Vāli while Sūrya fathers Sugrīva; no direct meeting is narrated.
Brahmā orders the gods to generate vāṇara champions, occasioning Sugrīva’s birth.
Vibhishana is Rāvaṇa’s younger brother.
After defecting, Vibhishana fights Rāvaṇa’s forces and smashes Rāvaṇa’s horses.
Rāvaṇa denounces and rejects Vibhishana for urging Sītā’s return.
Rāvaṇa kicks him, but Vibhishana grasps his feet and appeals again.
Vibhishana laments Rāvaṇa and performs his cremation at Rāma’s command.
Rāma accepts, protects and embraces Vibhishana despite the monkey chiefs’ suspicions.
Vibhishana advises Rāma, supplies intelligence and joins his campaign against Rāvaṇa.
Vibhishana accepts Rāma’s commands, performs Rāvaṇa’s funeral and rules Laṅkā.
Rāma gives Vibhishana the Raṅganātha image for his journey south.
Rāma shields Vibhishana from Rāvaṇa’s unfailing weapon.
Vibhishana supports her release and brings her to Rāma after victory.
Vibhishana prevents Rāvaṇa from executing Hanumān by invoking diplomatic law.
Hanumān argues that Vibhishana’s face and speech indicate sincerity.
Vibhishana and Hanumān fight together in the operation against Indrajit.
Kubera is Vibhishana’s paternal half-brother through Viśravas.
Brahmā grants steadfast righteousness, unlearned weapon knowledge and immortality.
Skanda and Vibhishana are named together in a Buddhist protective configuration.
Indra tests Yudhiṣṭhira's resolve by demanding that he abandon the dog.
Indra explains that Yudhiṣṭhira was deceived in return for deceiving Droṇa.
Sūrya grants Yudhiṣṭhira an inexhaustible food-vessel for his dependents.
Brahmā is present among the gods during Yudhiṣṭhira's final revelation.
Nārada advises Yudhiṣṭhira on marriage, celestial halls, sacrifice, and royal duty.
Nārada encounters Yudhiṣṭhira during the final heavenly episode.
Balarāma condemns Bhīma's unlawful blow within Yudhiṣṭhira's victorious coalition.
Yudhiṣṭhira learns Rāma's story from Mārkaṇḍeya rather than meeting him.

Agniveśa.note: He teaches Drona the fire weapon and its withdrawal.

Ahilāvatī.note: Regional genealogy identifies her as his wife, distinct from secure epic tradition.

Ajīgarta Sauyavasi.note: Hariścandra accepts Ajīgarta's sold middle son as substitute victim at the royal sacrifice.

Alambala.note: They battle with weapons, beasts, elements, mountains, and changing forms.
Ghaṭotkaca defeats and crushes the rākṣasa champion.

Alambuṣa.note: They oppose one another, though accounts vary across epic recensions.

Alāyudha.note: He counters and destroys Alāyudha’s supernatural warfare.
He beheads Alāyudha and presents the severed head before Duryodhana.

Amarka.note: Amarka joins Śaṇḍa in attempting to teach Prahlāda Daitya statecraft.

Ambarīṣa.note: Govindarāja identifies Hariścandra with the Rāmāyaṇa's purchasing king Ambarīṣa to reconcile conflicting accounts.

Ambikā.note: Bhīṣma abducts Ambikā and arranges her marriage to Vicitravīrya.
Ambikā is Duryodhana’s paternal grandmother through Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Ambā.note: Bhīṣma abducts Ambā, later releases her, and refuses her marriage request.

Ambālikā.note: Bhīṣma abducts Ambālikā and arranges her marriage to Vicitravīrya.

Antaboga.note: Wayang genealogies place Antaboga among Werkudara’s divine or serpentine in-laws.

Antareja.note: Javanese wayang genealogy makes Antareja a son of Werkudara.

Antasena.note: Javanese wayang genealogy makes Antasena a son of Werkudara.

Anuhlāda.note: Anuhlāda is listed among Prahlāda’s brothers.

Apaspati.note: Apaspati, alternatively Vasu, is Dhruva’s brother in Purāṇic variants.

Aravāṉ.note: His festival sacrifice occurs under Draupadī's ritual sovereignty.

Atri.note: Atri is named among the sages who instruct Dhruva.

Avalokiteśvara.note: Vibhishana shares guardian-deity space with Avalokiteśvara without genealogical identity.

Avindhya.note: The like-minded counsellor’s information reaches Sītā through Vibhishana’s household.

Ayaspati.note: Ayaspati is Dhruva’s brother in the Harivaṃśa genealogy.

Ayāsya.note: Ayāsya serves as Sāman-chanter during Hariścandra's sacrifice.

Añjanaparvan.note: Añjanaparvan is his only securely attested son in the critical epic.
Father and son fight for the Pāṇḍavas before Aśvatthāman kills Añjanaparvan.

Aśvapati.note: Aśvapati is Sāvitrī’s father and king of Madra.

Aśvasena.note: The Nāga survivor enters Karṇa’s arrow in an attempt to kill Arjuna.
Aśvasena enters or empowers Karṇa’s missile to avenge Khāṇḍava’s destruction.
Karṇa declines Aśvasena’s proposed second assisted attack against Arjuna.

Aśvatthāman.note: Aśvatthāman fights Abhimanyu and participates in destroying his weapons.
Arjuna repeatedly confronts his former fellow pupil and wartime enemy.
Bhīma fights Aśvatthāman and later pursues him after the night massacre.
Bhīṣma assesses Aśvatthāman, who serves as a champion under his command.
He kills her brother and five sons while attacking the sleeping camp.
She demands his jewel but ultimately supports sparing his life.
Aśvatthāman is Drona and Kṛpī’s son.
Drona secretly gives his son additional opportunities for martial instruction.

Aśvatthāman.myth: Night massacre of the Pāṇḍava camp
Aśvatthāman.note: Aśvatthāman massacres the sleeping camp and reports the vengeance to the rejoicing Duryodhana.
He attacks Aśvatthāman in anger after Aśvatthāman kills his son.
Karṇa and Aśvatthāman fight for Duryodhana despite quarrels over strategy and boasting.
Yudhiṣṭhira falsely implies that Droṇa's son Aśvatthāman has died.
Aśvatthāman murders Yudhiṣṭhira's son and nephews and becomes his postwar enemy.

Aśvins.note: Kuntī enables their invocation by teaching Mādrī the deity-summoning formula.

Aṅgada.myth: Aṅgada appointed heir and search leader
Aṅgada.note: Sugrīva supports his nephew’s appointment as heir and commands him in the southern search.
Some Jain accounts make Aṅgada a son of Sugrīva.
Aṅgada offers cautious advice about admitting Vibhishana into Rāma’s camp.
Aṅgada accompanies the force guided by Vibhishana against Indrajit.

Aṅgiras.note: Pallava pedigrees construct Aśvatthāman’s descent through Aṅgiras.
Aṅgiras is one of Dhruva’s instructing Seven Seers.

Babhruvāhana.note: Babhruvāhana is Arjuna’s son by Citrāṅgadā.
Arjuna rejects his son’s peaceful welcome and insists upon combat.
Babhruvāhana defeats and temporarily kills or renders Arjuna lifeless.

Baka.note: Bhīma eats Baka’s tribute, kills him, and leaves his corpse at the gate.
Kuntī arranges Baka’s destruction by volunteering Bhīma to confront the monster.

Balandharā.note: A Kāśī-princess genealogy names Balandharā as another wife of Bhīma.

Barbarīka.note: Later Purāṇic and cult traditions make Barbarīka his son.

Benyakai.note: Benyakai is Phiphek’s daughter in the Thai Ramakien.

Bhagadatta.note: Arjuna battles the elephant-mounted warrior and survives his Vaiṣṇava missile.
Arjuna kills Bhagadatta after Kṛṣṇa neutralizes the divine missile.
He encounters Bhagadatta as an opponent in qualified war traditions.

Bharadvāja.note: Aśvatthāman belongs to Bharadvāja’s lineage through Droṇa.
Bharadvāja’s semen, preserved in a vessel, generates Drona.
Bharadvāja participates in his son’s early education.

Bharata.note: Sugrīva meets Bharata’s royal household after returning victorious to Ayodhyā.

Bhramī.note: Bhramī is Dhruva’s wife and mother of Kalpa and Vatsara.

Bhurīśravas.note: Aśvatthāman attempts to support the Kaurava side around Bhurīśravas’s conflict.

Bhānumatī.note: Later Sanskrit drama names Bhānumatī as Duryodhana’s wife.

Bāṇa.note: Bāṇa, Bali’s eldest son, is Prahlāda’s great-grandson.

Bāṣkala.note: Some conflicting genealogical lists identify Bāṣkala as Prahlāda’s brother.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa alternatively names Bāṣkala as Prahlāda’s son.

Bṛhadaśva.note: Bṛhadaśva consoles Yudhiṣṭhira with Nala's story and teaches dice-lore.

Bṛhadbala of Kosala.note: Abhimanyu kills Bṛhadbala during his advance through the array.
A textually unstable retrospective also numbers Bṛhadbala among Abhimanyu’s surrounding attackers.

Bṛhaspati.note: Pallava pedigrees construct Aśvatthāman’s descent through Bṛhaspati.
Expanded later accounts list Bṛhaspati among Bhīṣma’s teachers.
Drona is born from a portion of the gods’ preceptor.

Candrasena.note: Yudhiṣṭhira fights the named warrior Candrasena in the war catalogues.

Cañcu.note: Cañcu or Campaka belongs to the later descendant line traced from Hariścandra.

Chyavana.note: Chyavana teaches Prahlāda about sacred places, prompting his pilgrimage.

Chāyā.myth: Endless clothing in Sāraḷā's dice hall
Chāyā.note: As a wife or power of Sūrya, she supplies Draupadī's inexhaustible clothing.

Citraratha.note: At Yudhiṣṭhira's request, the Gandharva releases the defeated Duryodhana.

Citrasena.note: The Gandharva Citrasena instructs Arjuna in celestial music and dance.
Citrasena defeats and captures Duryodhana during his expedition near the exiles.

Citrāṅgada.note: Citrāṅgada is Bhīṣma’s younger half-brother through Śantanu.
Bhīṣma installs and protects Citrāṅgada as Kuru king.

Citrāṅgada of Kaliṅga.note: Duryodhana carries away Citrāṅgada’s unnamed daughter after she passes him over.

Citrāṅgadā.note: Arjuna marries the princess under the condition that their son remain her kingdom’s heir.

Cārvāka.note: The disguised rākṣasa denounces Yudhiṣṭhira as a kin-killer before Brahmins destroy him.

Death.note: Aurobindo transforms Sāvitrī’s ordeal into a cosmic confrontation with personified Death.

Devikā.note: Devikā is Yudhiṣṭhira's other wife and mother of Yaudheya.

Devāśravas.note: An appended genealogy makes Devāśravas Ekalavya’s biological father.

Dewa Ruci.note: Bima encounters or enters the miniature deity, who reveals ultimate knowledge.

Dharma.note: Through Sūnṛtā, Dhruva is Dharma’s maternal descendant in the Harivaṃśa genealogy.
Dharma is said to circumambulate Dhruva’s imperishable station.

Dharma.myth: Multiplying garments in the dice hall
Dharma.note: Some witnesses attribute the protection of her clothing to Dharma.
Hariścandra serves Dharma unknowingly while Dharma assumes the form of his caṇḍāla master.
Dharma reveals his disguise and vindicates Hariścandra after the king completes the ordeal.
Kuntī invokes Dharma through Durvāsas’s formula and conceives Yudhiṣṭhira.
Dharma divinely fathers Yudhiṣṭhira through Kuntī's god-summoning mantra.

Dharma.myth: Yakṣa questions at the enchanted lake
Dharma.note: Disguised as a yakṣa, Dharma tests him and revives his brothers.
Dharma appears as a dog and tests his loyalty at heaven's threshold.

Dharma.myth: Illusory hell and final loyalty test
Dharma.note: Dharma reveals the hell vision as another test of Yudhiṣṭhira's loyalty.

Dhaumya.note: He offers to transport the Pāṇḍava priest with the party.
Dhaumya serves as family priest, conducts rites, and instructs the brothers.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra.note: Dhṛtarāṣṭra hears Saṃjaya’s narration of Abhimanyu’s battle and death.
Bhāsa makes Dhṛtarāṣṭra condemn or fear the consequences of Abhimanyu’s killing.
Kṛṣṇa substitutes an iron likeness when Dhṛtarāṣṭra attempts to crush Bhīma.
Bhīṣma raises and advises Dhṛtarāṣṭra and urges him to restrain Duryodhana.
Drona advises the royal patron and fights for his dynasty.
Duryodhana is his eldest son by Gāndhārī.
Duryodhana repeatedly pressures his reluctant father into supporting the dice match and war.
Gandhari is Dhṛtarāṣṭra's wife and blindfolds herself after learning of his blindness.
They retire together, practice austerities, and die beside each other in the forest fire.
As Kṛṣṇa’s envoy, he warns Dhṛtarāṣṭra of his sons’ destruction.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra permits the rigged dice disaster that dispossesses Yudhiṣṭhira.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra.myth: Restoration after the first dice game
Dhṛtarāṣṭra.note: Dhṛtarāṣṭra grants boons restoring Yudhiṣṭhira's freedom and wealth.
Yudhiṣṭhira maintains and honors Dhṛtarāṣṭra before permitting his retirement.

Dhṛti.note: Later genealogical summaries weakly attest Dhṛti as Prahlāda’s wife.

Dhṛṣṭadyumna.note: Arjuna’s brother-in-law commands and fights beside the Pāṇḍava army.

Dhṛṣṭadyumna.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Dhṛṣṭadyumna.note: Aśvatthāman wakes, beats, and kills Droṇa’s killer without granting a warrior’s death.
Bhīma supports the Pāṇḍava commander’s attacks upon Droṇa.
Her fire-born brother emerged from the same sacrificial rite.
Though born to kill him, Dhṛṣṭadyumna receives instruction within Drona’s school.

Dhṛṣṭadyumna.myth: Battle between teacher and destined killer
Dhṛṣṭadyumna.note: Dhṛṣṭadyumna fights Drona during the Kurukṣetra war.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna decapitates Drona after he lays down his weapons and enters yoga.
Karṇa clashes with the opposing commander Dhṛṣṭadyumna and counters his strategy.
Yudhiṣṭhira appoints Dhṛṣṭadyumna commander of his coalition.

Dhṛṣṭaketu.note: Dhṛṣṭaketu is named among Drona’s opponents in Book Seven.

Diti.note: Diti is Prahlāda’s paternal grandmother in Purāṇic genealogy.

Drupada.note: Arjuna defeats and captures Drupada as payment to Droṇa.
Drupada later becomes Arjuna’s father-in-law and political ally.
Drupada’s forces oppose Bhīṣma during the Kurukṣetra campaign.
Former companions become enemies when King Drupada rejects impoverished Drona as unequal.
Drona has his pupils capture Drupada and takes half his kingdom.
Drona kills his former friend and enemy during the Kurukṣetra war.
Drupada negotiates Yudhiṣṭhira's unusual marriage and later fights for his cause.

Dundubhi.note: Sugrīva uses the dead demon’s skeleton to test Rāma’s strength.

Durjaya.note: Aśvatthāman installs Duryodhana’s son Durjaya as king.
Bhāsa portrays Durjaya as Duryodhana’s young son, distinct from securely attested Lakṣmaṇa.
The dying Duryodhana embraces and instructs his young son.
Bhāsa's drama presents the young child as Gandhari's grandson.
The child joins Gandhari and Dhṛtarāṣṭra beside the dying Duryodhana.

Durvāsas.myth: Durvāsas arrives after Draupadī has eaten
Durvāsas.note: His visit threatens the household until Kṛṣṇa intervenes in the devotional variant.
Durvāsas curses Śakuntalā to be forgotten after she neglects his reception.
Durvāsas arrives with disciples after eating, threatening the exiles with his anger.

Duryodhana's queens.note: Gandhari shares the dying Duryodhana's battlefield scene with his queens.

Duḥśāsana.note: Abhimanyu defeats or forces Duḥśāsana away during the battle.
Arjuna opposes Draupadī’s assailant during the wider Kaurava conflict.
Bhīma kills Duḥśāsana, tears open his chest, and tastes or drinks his blood.
Bhīṣma tells Duḥśāsana that the devastating arrows striking him are Arjuna’s.
He drags her by the hair and attempts to remove her garment.
Duḥśāsana is among the Kaurava pupils trained by Drona.
Duḥśāsana fights within the Kaurava forces and battle structures Drona commands.
Duḥśāsana is Duryodhana’s closest brother and principal agent.

Duḥśāsana.myth: Draupadī’s coercion in the dice hall
Duḥśāsana.note: At Duryodhana’s direction, Duḥśāsana drags Draupadī into the assembly.
Duḥśāsana is one of Gandhari's sons.
She laments his mutilated corpse and Bhīma's apparent drinking of his blood.
Duḥśāsana is ordered to protect Karṇa from Ghaṭotkaca.

Duḥśāsana.myth: Draupadī's humiliation in the dice hall
Duḥśāsana.note: Duḥśāsana drags and attempts to strip Draupadī while Yudhiṣṭhira is enslaved.

Duḥśāsana’s son.note: After both fall, Duḥśāsana’s son rises first and fatally strikes Abhimanyu.

Dvāpara.note: Dvāpara inhabits Puṣkara's dice, contributing to Nala's loss of kingdom.

Dyau.note: One variable tradition identifies Bhīṣma’s divine identity as the Vasu Dyau.

Dyumatsena.note: Dyumatsena is Satyavān’s father, the blinded and dispossessed Śālva king.

Earth.note: The earth seizes Karṇa’s wheel in fulfillment of the Brahmin owner’s curse.
Later folklore makes Earth personally curse Karṇa after he injures or squeezes her.

Gandharva Citrasena.note: Citrasena’s Gandharvas defeat the Kaurava expedition, forcing Karṇa to withdraw.

Gaṇeśa.note: A local temple tradition says Śakuntalā worshipped Gaṇeśa at Kaṇva’s direction.
Gaṇeśa and Vibhishana are named together in a Buddhist protective configuration.

Ghṛtācī.note: Her appearance stimulates Bharadvāja’s emission, indirectly causing Drona’s birth.
Later summaries simplify Ghṛtācī’s role by treating her as Drona’s mother.

Goddess Sāvitrī.note: The goddess procures and announces Sāvitrī’s birth but is not her biological mother.

Guha.myth: Variant direction of Rāma toward Sugrīva
Guha.note: Some later traditions have Guha redirect Rāma toward Sugrīva; no personal encounter is secure.

Harita.note: Harita is Hariścandra's later descendant through Rohita in the dominant Purāṇic genealogy.

Hiraṇyadhanuṣ.note: The critical epic identifies Ekalavya as Hiraṇyadhanuṣ’s son.
A secondary genealogy makes Hiraṇyadhanuṣ Ekalavya’s adoptive rather than biological father.

Hiraṇyakaśipu.note: Prahlāda is consistently identified as Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son.
His father repeatedly attempts to kill him for worshipping Viṣṇu.
Hiraṇyakaśipu recognizes Viṣṇu’s power and embraces Prahlāda.

Hiḍimba.note: Bhīma wrestles and kills the cannibal rākṣasa Hiḍimba.
Hiḍimba is his maternal uncle, killed before Ghaṭotkaca’s birth.

Hiḍimbā.note: Hiḍimbā desires Bhīma, warns him, and becomes his temporary partner.
Hiḍimbā bears Ghaṭotkaca after her temporary union with Bhīma.
At his mother’s request, he seeks a human meal.
Hiḍimbā appeals to Kuntī, who authorizes a conditional union with Bhīma.

Holikā.myth: Holikā enters the pyre with Prahlāda
Holikā.note: Prahlāda survives when his fire-protected aunt attempts to burn him.
Holikā.source: Late festival literature and regional tradition

Hrāda.note: Hrāda is listed among Prahlāda’s brothers.

Ilā.note: Ilā is Dhruva’s wife and mother of Utkala and a daughter.

Indrajit.note: Indrajit is Vibhishana’s nephew through his brother Rāvaṇa.
Indrajit shoots Vibhishana, who kills his horses and enables Lakṣmaṇa’s victory.
Vibhishana reveals Indrajit’s vulnerability and urges attack before his rite is completed.

Irāvat.note: Irāvat is Arjuna’s son by Ulūpī.

Jamadagni.note: Jamadagni officiates as adhvaryu at Hariścandra's sacrifice without a separate adventure.

Jarasandha.note: Jarasandha pursues or opposes the abduction while Karṇa fights for Duryodhana.
Retrospective traditions credit Karṇa with combat against Jarasandha; details vary.
Some retrospective traditions connect Karṇa with Jarasandha as an ally after combat.

Jarāsandha.note: Jarāsandha chooses Bhīma for single combat after the disguised entry into Magadha.
Bhīma kills Jarāsandha by breaking his body with Kṛṣṇa’s guidance.
Later synthesis portrays Ekalavya as Jarāsandha’s ally or subordinate.
Yudhiṣṭhira authorizes the mission in which Bhīma kills his imperial obstacle.

Jatāsura.note: Bhīma kills the disguised rākṣasa after he abducts Draupadī and Pāṇḍavas.

Jayadratha.note: Jayadratha blocks Abhimanyu’s supporters, leaving him isolated among enemy warriors.
Arjuna pursues Jayadratha for blocking aid to the doomed Abhimanyu.
Arjuna decapitates Jayadratha with a specialized shot before sunset.
Bhīma captures and brutalizes Jayadratha, but Yudhiṣṭhira prevents his killing.
He propositions and forcibly abducts her after she refuses him.
Drona’s deployment enables Jayadratha to bar the pursuing Pāṇḍavas.
Duryodhana and Droṇa protect their Kuru ally after Abhimanyu’s death.
Jayadratha is Gandhari's son-in-law through his marriage to Duḥśalā.
She views and laments her son-in-law among the war dead.
After Jayadratha's capture, Yudhiṣṭhira spares him but subjects him to humiliation.

Jayananda.note: Some Jain accounts name Jayananda as Sugrīva’s son.

Jāmbavān.myth: Mobilization of the southern search party
Jāmbavān.note: Sugrīva summons the senior bear-chief and assigns him to the southern search.
Jāmbavān advises caution when Vibhishana requests admission to Rāma’s camp.
Jāmbavān joins Vibhishana in the operation against Indrajit.

Jīmūta.note: Bhīma wrestles Jīmūta before Virāṭa’s court for public entertainment.
Bhīma whirls Jīmūta and dashes him to death.

Kabandha.note: Kabandha recommends Sugrīva to Rāma, though Sugrīva never personally meets him.

Kaikasī.note: Kaikasī is Vibhishana’s mother in Vālmīki’s later genealogy.

Kalabendana.note: Javanese wayang connects Kalabendana with Abimanyu’s expanded marriage and death cycle.

Kalpa.note: Kalpa is Dhruva’s son by Bhramī.

Kamakaṭaṅkaṭā.note: A later Purāṇic cycle makes Muru’s daughter his wife or consort.

Karkoṭaka.note: Nala rescues the immobilized nāga king from a forest fire.
Karkoṭaka bites Nala, disguising him as the misshapen Bāhuka.
Karkoṭaka gives Nala garments that later restore his true form.

Kauravas.note: Gandhari is mother of the one hundred Kaurava sons.
She repeatedly counsels the Kauravas through Duryodhana against their hostility and war policy.
She mourns all one hundred sons after their slaughter.

Kayādhu.note: Kayādhu carries Prahlāda while receiving Nārada’s protection and teaching.

Kaśyapa.note: Kaśyapa is said to circumambulate Dhruva’s imperishable station.
Kaśyapa is Prahlāda’s paternal grandfather in Purāṇic genealogy.

Kirmīra.note: Bhīma kills Kirmīra, a rākṣasa related to Baka or Hiḍimba.

Kratu.note: Kratu is one of Dhruva’s instructing Seven Seers.

Kumbha.note: Variant Purāṇic lists name Kumbha as Prahlāda’s son.
Sugrīva kills Kumbha after a prolonged combat.

Kumbhakarṇa.note: Kumbhakarṇa knocks Sugrīva unconscious; Sugrīva revives, mutilates his face, and escapes.
Both condemn Rāvaṇa, but Vibhishana defects while Kumbhakarṇa fights from familial loyalty.
Vibhishana approaches Kumbhakarṇa and unsuccessfully tries to save him from death.

Kāla.note: Personified Time announces invisibly that the earth is swallowing Karṇa’s wheel.

Kālakeyas.note: Arjuna battles the Kālakeya demons during his celestial career.
Arjuna defeats and destroys the Kālakeya host.

Kīcaka.note: Bhīma replaces Draupadī at the assignation, kills Kīcaka, and mutilates his corpse.
He sexually coerces, pursues, and publicly kicks Draupadī.

Kīcaka.myth: Night meeting in the dance hall
Kīcaka.note: Draupadī lures him to a meeting where Bhīma waits and kills him.

Kīrtimant.note: Kīrtimant is Dhruva’s brother in the one-wife genealogy.

Kūṣmāṇḍa deities.note: The Kūṣmāṇḍas create terrifying illusions against the meditating Dhruva.

Kṛpa.note: Kṛpa fights Abhimanyu and helps disable his chariot crew and surround him.
Kṛpa is one of Arjuna’s martial teachers.
Arjuna faces his former teacher as a Kaurava battlefield opponent.
Kṛpa, Kṛpī’s twin brother, is Aśvatthāman’s maternal uncle.

Kṛpa.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Kṛpa.note: Kṛpa counsels against the raid but later guards an exit and kills fugitives.
Kṛpa serves as Bhīma’s teacher and elder before becoming a war opponent.
Bhīma fights Kṛpa during the Kurukṣetra conflict.
Kṛpa serves as Bhīṣma’s fellow Kaurava combatant and attends his arrow-bed.
His brother-in-law fights beside him and receives Drona’s final warning.
Kṛpa is one of Duryodhana’s martial teachers.
Kṛpa survives the war and attends the mortally wounded Duryodhana.
Kṛpa demands Karṇa’s royal lineage before permitting combat with Arjuna.
Kṛpa is one of Yudhiṣṭhira's martial teachers.
Kṛpa gives a prewar blessing, then fights Yudhiṣṭhira's coalition.
Yudhiṣṭhira retains the surviving Kṛpa as Parikṣit's teacher.

Kṛpī.note: Kṛpī is Drona’s wife and ritual partner.

Kṛtavarman.note: Kṛtavarman kills Abhimanyu’s horses and joins the surrounding attack.
Arjuna confronts the Vṛṣṇi warrior fighting for the Kauravas.

Kṛtavarman.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Kṛtavarman.note: Kṛtavarman guards the camp exits and kills fugitives during Aśvatthāman’s raid.
The Yādava warrior accompanies Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa to the dying Duryodhana.
Kṛtavarman fights Yudhiṣṭhira and his forces during the war.

Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa is Abhimanyu’s maternal uncle and an ally of his family.
A folk variant makes Kṛṣṇa the instructor who deliberately stops the fetal lesson.
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna jointly help Agni burn the forest.
Kṛṣṇa teaches Arjuna duty, disciplined action, knowledge, devotion, and divine embodiment.
Kṛṣṇa chooses to serve as Arjuna’s unarmed charioteer.
Kṛṣṇa neutralizes Bhagadatta’s divine missile before it can destroy Arjuna.
Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa form the human manifestation of the primordial pair.
Kṛṣṇa frustrates Aśvatthāman’s earlier effort to obtain his discus.
Kṛṣṇa condemns him to diseased, solitary wandering for three thousand years.
Kṛṣṇa repeatedly chooses, counsels, provokes, and strategically supports Bhīma.
Kṛṣṇa signals how Bhīma should break Jarāsandha’s body apart.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Strategy for the final mace duel
Kṛṣṇa.note: Kṛṣṇa explains that Bhīma cannot defeat Duryodhana by fighting fairly.
Kṛṣṇa rushes to attack Bhīṣma until Arjuna restrains him.
Kṛṣṇa leads Yudhiṣṭhira to Bhīṣma and validates the dying elder’s teaching.
Kṛṣṇa consoles Gaṅgā by recalling Bhīṣma’s Vasu nature and heroic death.
Kṛṣṇa devises the deception intended to make the undefeated Drona disarm.
Kṛṣṇa is among the few said to perceive Drona’s spiritual departure.
Duryodhana rejects Kṛṣṇa’s diplomacy and plots to seize him.
Kṛṣṇa advises the prohibited strategy that allows Bhīma to defeat Duryodhana.

Kṛṣṇa.myth: Duryodhana’s accusation after the thigh blow
Kṛṣṇa.note: Duryodhana accuses Kṛṣṇa of engineering unfair deaths; Kṛṣṇa answers with his crimes.
Later epic notices describe Ekalavya repeatedly challenging Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa kills Ekalavya, removing a warrior later portrayed as threatening the Pāṇḍavas.
An appended Yādava genealogy makes Ekalavya a cousin of Kṛṣṇa.
Guided by Kṛṣṇa, Gandhari supernaturally surveys and narrates the corpse-strewn battlefield.
She accuses Kṛṣṇa of permitting a slaughter he had the power to prevent.
She curses Kṛṣṇa to lose his clan and die ingloriously without his kin.
He obeys Kṛṣṇa’s commands to attack Karṇa and then Alāyudha.
Kṛṣṇa celebrates his strategic death and says he otherwise would have killed him.
Kṛṣṇa sends him as an envoy to warn the Kuru court.
Kṛṣṇa reveals Karṇa’s birth and offers the Pāṇḍava throne if he defects.
Kṛṣṇa rejects Karṇa’s appeal to combat law and orders Arjuna’s fatal shot.
Disguised Kṛṣṇa receives the dying Karṇa’s accumulated merit of generosity.
Kuntī is Kṛṣṇa’s paternal aunt in the dominant Vṛṣṇi genealogy.
Kṛṣṇa visits Kuntī, knows Karṇa’s birth, and carries her message to her sons.
Kuntī praises Kṛṣṇa as the supreme being and asks for freedom from familial attachment.
Vibhishana acknowledges the rājasūya enterprise associated with Kṛṣṇa and the Pandavas.
Kṛṣṇa is Yudhiṣṭhira's cousin, political ally, counsellor, and divine guide.
Yudhiṣṭhira follows Kṛṣṇa's strategy and deceives Droṇa about Aśvatthāman's death.

Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.myth: Draupadī demands vengeance before the embassy
Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.note: He hears her lament, promises vengeance, and supports pursuit of Aśvatthāman.

Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.myth: Endless-cloth protection in the dice hall
Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.note: Later devotional versions make Kṛṣṇa miraculously supply her endless clothing.

Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.myth: Durvāsas visits after Draupadī has eaten
Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva.note: Kṛṣṇa eats a remaining morsel, supernaturally satisfying Durvāsas and his disciples.

Lakṣmaṇa.note: Lakṣmaṇa accompanies Rāma in the compact and subsequent campaign with Sugrīva.
Lakṣmaṇa enters Kiṣkindhā angrily and threatens punishment when Sugrīva delays the search.
Vibhishana guides and supports Lakṣmaṇa during the attack on Indrajit.
Lakṣmaṇa intervenes when Rāvaṇa attacks Vibhishana and receives the redirected spear.
Lakṣmaṇa provisionally anoints him and later consecrates him king of Laṅkā.

Lakṣmaṇa Kumāra.note: Lakṣmaṇa Kumāra is Gandhari's grandson through Duryodhana.
She mourns her grandson with the other fallen Kauravas.
He impersonates the bride and humiliates the prospective bridegroom.

Lakṣmaṇa, son of Duryodhana.note: Abhimanyu kills Lakṣmaṇa with an arrow, intensifying Duryodhana’s rage.

Lakṣmaṇā.note: Later Kṛṣṇa-family tradition makes Lakṣmaṇā Duryodhana’s daughter.

Lakṣmī.note: A television adaptation has Lakṣmī personally rescue and protect Dhruva.
Lakṣmī hesitates to approach Narasiṃha; Prahlāda approaches after her.

Lomaśa.note: Lomaśa reports Arjuna’s celestial progress while guiding the exiled Pāṇḍavas.
His rākṣasa companions transport the sage with the expedition.
Lomaśa guides Yudhiṣṭhira's pilgrimage and transmits divine messages.

Madanī.note: The Amarāvatī pedigree makes the apsaras Madanī Aśvatthāman’s consort.

Madhva.note: Bhīma and Madhva are successive manifestations of Vāyu in Dvaita theology.

Mainda.note: Mainda gives his opinion when Rāma’s allies debate admitting Vibhishana.

Maitreya.note: Maitreya’s curse predicts that Bhīma will break Duryodhana’s thigh.
After Duryodhana contemptuously displays his thigh, Maitreya curses Bhīma to break it.
Maitreya visits Yudhiṣṭhira's party before later cursing Duryodhana.

Malyavān.note: Malyavān and Vibhishana both advise Rāvaṇa to pursue peace.

Mandodarī.note: Mandodarī is Vibhishana’s sister-in-law as Rāvaṇa’s wife.
Some later traditions make Vibhishana marry Mandodarī after Rāvaṇa’s death.

Marīca.note: Marīca shelters Śakuntalā and her son after her rejection.
Marīca explains Durvāsas’s curse when Śakuntalā and Duṣyanta reunite.

Marīci.note: Marīci participates in teaching Dhruva worship and mantra.

Mataṅga.note: Mataṅga’s curse bars Vāli from Ṛṣyamūka, indirectly providing Sugrīva a refuge.

Maya.note: Arjuna protects Maya from death during the forest conflagration.
Maya repays Arjuna’s protection by building the Pāṇḍavas’ wondrous hall.
Maya builds the extraordinary hall that becomes Yudhiṣṭhira's imperial court.

Maṇimān.note: Bhīma kills the yakṣa or rākṣasa guardian Maṇimān.

Meghavarṇa.note: Regional and popular works sometimes list Meghavarṇa as his son.

Menakā.note: Menakā, manifested as a radiant power, carries away her rejected daughter.

Mādrī.note: Mādrī is his stepmother and mother of Nakula and Sahadeva.

Mālavī.note: Bhāsa names Mālavī as one of Duryodhana’s wives.
Mālavī attends Duryodhana as he dies from his shattered thighs.
Mālavī is Sāvitrī’s mother and Aśvapati’s chief queen.

Mālinī.note: Mālinī is Vibhishana’s mother in the competing Mahābhārata genealogy.

Mārkaṇḍeya.note: Mārkaṇḍeya narrates the couple’s story but never meets them within it.
Mārkaṇḍeya answers Yudhiṣṭhira's questions through extensive embedded stories.

Mātali.note: Mātali transports Duṣyanta to Marīca’s hermitage, enabling reunion with Śakuntalā.
Both assist Rāma’s victory; Mātali gives the final Brahmā-missile prompt.

Māyā.myth: Endless clothing in Sāraḷā's dice hall
Māyā.note: As a wife or power of Sūrya, she supplies Draupadī's inexhaustible clothing.

Māyāvin.note: Māyāvin’s cave combat causes Sugrīva’s mistaken succession and ensuing exile.

Mūka.note: Arjuna and Śiva both shoot the demon appearing as a boar.

Mṛtyu.note: Dhruva steps on Death’s head as a stair into the celestial vehicle.

Nagagini.note: Wayang genealogies make the serpentine Nagagini a wife of Werkudara.

Nahusha.note: Nahusha overpowers and captures Bhīma, whose physical strength proves useless.

Nakula.note: Nakula joins the force trying unsuccessfully to follow Abhimanyu.
Nakula is Arjuna’s Pāṇḍava brother and fellow husband of Draupadī.
Nakula and Arjuna act together as Pāṇḍava allies.
Nakula is Bhīma’s paternal half-brother through Pāṇḍu’s wife Mādrī.
Bhīṣma advises Nakula as one of the Pāṇḍavas.
One of her five husbands and father of Śatānīka.
Drona teaches Nakula as a Kuru prince.
Nakula later fights against Drona’s army.
Duryodhana’s dice scheme reduces his cousin Nakula to a claimed slave.
Nakula fights against Duryodhana’s Kuru coalition.

Nakula.myth: The princes discover the arrow-filled dog
Nakula.note: Nakula is among the princes whose dog reveals Ekalavya’s extraordinary archery.
Nakula joins the Pāṇḍavas seeking reconciliation and later honors the Kuru elders.
His followers transport Nakula, who later fights beside him.
Karṇa is Nakula’s elder maternal half-brother.
Karṇa defeats but spares Nakula under his promise to Kuntī.
After Mādrī’s death, Kuntī raises Nakula as one of her five sons.
Nakula is Yudhiṣṭhira's younger paternal and social half-brother.

Nakula.myth: Choice of one brother at the lake
Nakula.note: Yudhiṣṭhira chooses Nakula's revival to preserve Mādrī's line impartially.

Nanda.note: Viṣṇu’s attendant brings the celestial vehicle and addresses Dhruva.

Nara.note: The epic identifies Arjuna as the earthly manifestation or rebirth of Nara.
Prahlāda fights Nara before recognizing the pair’s divine power.

Nikumbha.note: Variant Purāṇic lists name Nikumbha as Prahlāda’s son.

Nivātakavacas.note: Arjuna fights the Asura host on Indra’s commission.
Arjuna destroys the Nivātakavacas for Indra.

Niwātakawaca.note: Arjuna fights the Javanese demon king during his celestial mission.
Arjuna defeats and kills the demon king in the Javanese poem.

Nārāyaṇa.note: Arjuna as Nara is cosmically paired with Nārāyaṇa, identified with Kṛṣṇa.
Aśvatthāman deploys a weapon associated with Nārāyaṇa, without meeting the deity.
Prahlāda fights the ascetic Nārāyaṇa before recognizing his divine power.
Yudhiṣṭhira beholds Kṛṣṇa in transcendent Nārāyaṇa form in heaven.

Nīla.myth: Search for Sītā and Laṅkā war
Nīla.note: Nīla commands forces under Sugrīva during the search and war.

One hundred Mālavas.note: Aśvapati and Mālavī’s one hundred sons are Sāvitrī’s brothers.

One hundred sons.note: Yama promises Sāvitrī one hundred strong sons by Satyavān.

Pallava.note: The Amarāvatī pedigree makes Aśvatthāman and Madanī parents of Pallava.
A competing pedigree derives Pallava from Aśvatthāman and a Nāga princess.

Paraśurāma.note: The epic presents Paraśurāma as Bhīṣma’s teacher or senior martial authority.
Bhīṣma fights Paraśurāma over Ambā for days without a decisive victor.
Paraśurāma transmits martial knowledge and secret weapon formulas to Drona.
Having distributed his wealth, Paraśurāma gives Drona his weapons.
Paraśurāma teaches Karṇa after Karṇa represents himself as a Brahmin.
Karṇa conceals his warrior status to obtain Paraśurāma’s weapon instruction.
Paraśurāma curses Karṇa to forget crucial weapon knowledge at his decisive hour.

Parikṣit.note: Parikṣit is Abhimanyu’s posthumous son and continues the Kuru dynasty.
Arjuna is Parikṣit’s grandfather through Abhimanyu and Uttarā.
Parikṣit is Yudhiṣṭhira's grandnephew through Arjuna and Abhimanyu.
Yudhiṣṭhira installs Parikṣit on the Kuru throne before departing.

Parīkṣit.myth: Brahmaśiras attack on the unborn heir
Parīkṣit.note: Aśvatthāman’s weapon strikes Parīkṣit in utero, causing him to be born dead.

Pauravī.note: Bhāsa names Pauravī as one of Duryodhana’s wives.
Pauravī attends Duryodhana as he dies from his shattered thighs.

Pañcāla/Sṛñjaya leaders.note: Drona fights and kills leaders of the Pañcāla and Sṛñjaya coalition.

Prabhāsa.note: Later systematized tradition identifies Bhīṣma’s divine identity as the Vasu Prabhāsa.

Pradyumna.note: Later tradition names Pradyumna among Abhimanyu’s martial trainers.
Ekalavya and Pradyumna exchange arrows and mace attacks in appended battle narratives.

Prahasta.note: Prahasta opposes Vibhishana as a counsellor and commander loyal to Rāvaṇa.

Prativindhya.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Prativindhya.note: Aśvatthāman kills Draupadī and Yudhiṣṭhira’s son during the raid.
Her son by Yudhiṣṭhira, later killed in the night raid.
Prativindhya is Yudhiṣṭhira's son by Draupadī.

Pulaha.note: Pulaha is one of Dhruva’s instructing Seven Seers.

Pulastya.note: Pulastya is one of Dhruva’s instructing Seven Seers.
Vibhishana is Pulastya’s grandson through Viśravas.

Purocana.note: Purocana constructs and guards the combustible house for Duryodhana’s faction.

Pāṇḍu.note: Arjuna is socially and dynastically Pāṇḍu’s legal son.
Pāṇḍu is Bhīma’s social and dynastic father and authorizes divine generation.
Bhīṣma raises Pāṇḍu, installs him, and arranges his marriage.
Jain Digambara tradition makes Pāṇḍu, rather than Sūrya, Karṇa’s father.
Pāṇḍu is Yudhiṣṭhira's legal and socially recognized father.
Nārada reports Pāṇḍu's wish that Yudhiṣṭhira perform the rājasūya.

Pōtturāja.note: He serves as her brother-like guardian, boundary attendant, and temple protector.

Raṅganātha.note: Vibhishana transports the image until it settles at Śrīraṅgam facing Laṅkā.

Rohita.note: Rohita is Hariścandra's son and successor in Vedic, Purāṇic, and regional traditions.

Rohita.myth: Rohita promised as Varuṇa's human victim
Rohita.note: Hariścandra promises his son as sacrifice, repeatedly delays, then accepts Śunaḥśepa as substitute.

Rohitāśva.note: Hariścandra sells Rohitāśva with Śaivyā to meet Viśvāmitra's demanded priestly fee.
Hariścandra's intended self-immolation precedes divine restoration of his dead son and installation as king.

Rukmaratha.note: Abhimanyu kills Śalya’s son Rukmaratha during the battle.

Rukmin.note: Rukmin pursues or opposes the abduction while Karṇa fights for Duryodhana.

Rumā.note: Rumā is Sugrīva’s wife, seized by Vāli and restored afterward.

Sahadeva.note: Sahadeva joins the force trying unsuccessfully to follow Abhimanyu.
Sahadeva is Arjuna’s Pāṇḍava brother and fellow husband of Draupadī.
Sahadeva and Arjuna act together as Pāṇḍava allies.
Sahadeva is Bhīma’s paternal half-brother through Pāṇḍu’s wife Mādrī.
Bhīṣma advises Sahadeva as one of the Pāṇḍavas.
One of her five husbands and father of Śrutasena.
Drona teaches Sahadeva as a Kuru prince.
Sahadeva later fights against Drona’s army.
Duryodhana’s dice scheme reduces his cousin Sahadeva to a claimed slave.
Sahadeva fights against Duryodhana’s Kuru coalition.

Sahadeva.myth: The princes discover the arrow-filled dog
Sahadeva.note: Sahadeva is among the princes whose dog reveals Ekalavya’s extraordinary archery.
Sahadeva joins the Pāṇḍavas seeking reconciliation and later serves the Kuru elders.
His followers transport Sahadeva, who later fights beside him.
Karṇa is Sahadeva’s elder maternal half-brother.
Karṇa fights Sahadeva but observes his promise not to kill Kuntī’s younger sons.
After Mādrī’s death, Kuntī raises Sahadeva as one of her five sons.
Calling Sahadeva especially dear, Kuntī asks Yudhiṣṭhira to care for him.
Vibhishana answers Sahadeva’s mediated request by sending tribute through Ghaṭotkaca.
Sahadeva is Yudhiṣṭhira's younger paternal and social half-brother.

Sahasrakavaca.note: Later synthesis identifies Karṇa as the reincarnation of the thousand-armored demon.

Saman.note: Saman and Vibhishana are named together in a Buddhist protective configuration.

Saramā.note: Saramā, daughter of Śailūṣa, is named as Vibhishana’s wife.

Sarvaga.note: Sarvaga is Bhīma’s son in the Kāśī-princess genealogy.

Satyabhāmā.note: Draupadī rejects magical husband-control and teaches her demanding household ethic.

Satyavatī.note: Bhīṣma renounces succession and offspring so Satyavatī’s descendants may rule.
Bhīṣma refuses Satyavatī’s request to take the throne or engender heirs.

Saṃhlāda.note: Saṃhlāda is listed among Prahlāda’s brothers.

Saṃjaya.note: Saṃjaya narrates Abhimanyu’s battle and death without meeting him in combat.
The court attendant serves Gandhari and Dhṛtarāṣṭra and accompanies them into the forest.

Saṃśaptakas.note: The sworn enemies repeatedly draw Arjuna away from the central battle.

Subala.note: Gandhari is the daughter of Subala, king of Gandhāra.

Subhadrā.note: Later tradition says the fetus learns entry before Subhadrā falls asleep.
Arjuna abducts and marries Kṛṣṇa’s sister, who bears Abhimanyu.

Sunanda.note: Sunanda accompanies Nanda in conveying Dhruva bodily to Viṣṇu’s station.

Sunīti.note: Sunīti is Dhruva’s mother in the two-wife narrative genealogy.
She teaches Dhruva karma, virtue and devotion after his rejection.

Sunīti.myth: Mother and son attain celestial stations
Sunīti.note: She receives a nearby celestial place and, later, ascends ahead of Dhruva.

Suprabhā.note: Suprabhā is connected with Arjuna’s mission and heavenly marriage in Javanese tradition.

Suruci.myth: Suruci rejects Dhruva from the royal lap
Suruci.note: His stepmother denies his fitness for the lap and directs him toward divine favor.

Sutasoma.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Sutasoma.note: Sutasoma wounds Aśvatthāman before Aśvatthāman kills him.
Sutasoma is Bhīma’s son by Draupadī.
Her son by Bhīma, later killed in the night raid.

Suśarman.note: Arjuna defeats the Trigarta opponent in the cattle raid and war.

Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.note: Dhruva is the grandson of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
Manu condemns Dhruva’s collective vengeance and orders him to stop killing.

Sāmba.note: Sāmba abducts Duryodhana’s daughter, provoking conflict between the Kurus and Yādavas.

Sāraṇa.note: Vibhishana detects or identifies Sāraṇa while he spies in Rāma’s camp.

Sātyaki.note: Sātyaki attempts to follow Abhimanyu but Jayadratha holds him back.
Some later summaries name Sātyaki as Abhimanyu’s trainer.
The Vṛṣṇi archer supports Arjuna and the Pāṇḍava side.
Aśvatthāman repeatedly fights Sātyaki, who later escapes the massacre by being absent.
Bhīma and Sātyaki fight beside one another and exchange battlefield support.
Sātyaki repeatedly duels, checks, or bypasses Drona while advancing.
Sātyaki appears on the opposing Yādava side; direct contact varies between appended passages.
Sātyaki is assigned as his rear guard and support against Karṇa.
Karṇa repeatedly clashes with Sātyaki during the war.
Sātyaki fights as Yudhiṣṭhira's ally and is repeatedly dispatched or protected by him.

Sūnṛtā.note: Sūnṛtā is Dhruva’s mother in the one-wife epic-supplement genealogy.
Purāṇic genealogical variants likewise name Sūnṛtā as Dhruva’s mother.

Takṣaka.note: Arjuna burns Takṣaka’s forest while the serpent king is absent.

The Upapāṇḍavas.note: Abhimanyu’s cousins fight beside him as fellow young Pāṇḍava warriors.

Trijaṭā.note: Medieval commentary and regional Ramayanas identify Trijaṭā as Vibhishana’s daughter.
The Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa may identify Trijaṭā as Vibhishana’s wife.
Some traditions identify Trijaṭā as Vibhishana’s sister.

Triśaṅku.note: Triśaṅku is Hariścandra's father in the dominant Purāṇic solar-dynasty genealogy.

Tārā.note: Vāli’s widow joins Sugrīva’s household and exercises political authority; traditions dispute her marital status.

Tārā.myth: Lakṣmaṇa confronts Sugrīva over his delay
Tārā.note: Tārā mediates when an enraged Lakṣmaṇa enters Kiṣkindhā threatening Sugrīva.

Ugrāyudha Paurava.note: Bhīṣma kills Ugrāyudha after he demands Satyavatī following Śantanu’s death.

Ulūpī.note: The Nāga princess pressures Arjuna into intercourse and bears Irāvat.
Ulūpī overcomes Arjuna’s stated reluctance through pressure and argument.
Ulūpī restores Arjuna after Babhruvāhana defeats and kills him.

Unnamed Nāga princess.note: Competing Pallava genealogies give Aśvatthāman an unnamed Nāga princess as consort.

Upakīcakas.note: They bind Draupadī to the corpse and try to burn her alive.

Urangayu.note: Javanese wayang traditions give Werkudara an additional wife named Urangayu.

Urvāśī.note: Urvaśī propositions Arjuna, who refuses her as a revered ancestress.
After his rejection, Urvaśī curses Arjuna to lose masculinity or live among women.

Utkala.note: Utkala is Dhruva’s son by Ilā.
Dhruva installs Utkala as successor before retiring to Badarikāśrama.

Uttama.note: Uttama is Dhruva’s favored half-brother in the two-wife genealogy.

Uttama.myth: Uttama’s death provokes the Yakṣa war
Uttama.note: Dhruva wages indiscriminate war after a Yakṣa kills Uttama.

Uttara.note: Arjuna initially serves as Uttara’s charioteer, then wins the battle.
Arjuna steadies the frightened prince and defeats the attacking Kuru champions.

Uttara, son of Virāṭa.note: Uttara is Abhimanyu’s brother-in-law within the Matsya alliance.

Uttarā.note: Abhimanyu marries Uttarā, who bears his posthumous son Parikṣit.
Disguised as Bṛhannalā, Arjuna teaches Uttarā music and dance.
Aśvatthāman directs his unrecalled weapon against Uttarā’s womb.
Yudhiṣṭhira participates as dynastic elder in the marriage sealing Virāṭa's alliance.

Uttānapāda.note: Dhruva is Uttānapāda’s son in every recorded genealogy.
He denies Dhruva his lap, later embraces him and relinquishes kingship.

Uśanas.note: Uśanas praises Dhruva’s austerity and Sunīti’s resulting exaltation.

Vajra.note: Yudhiṣṭhira establishes Vajra in Yādava territory before departing.

Varcas.note: The epic explicitly identifies Abhimanyu as Varcas embodied in human form.

Vasiṣṭha.note: Vasiṣṭha’s curse condemns Bhīṣma and the other Vasus to human birth.
Later accounts count Vasiṣṭha among Devavrata’s formal teachers.
Vasiṣṭha is one of Dhruva’s instructing Seven Seers.
Vasiṣṭha belongs to the defined priestly team officiating at Hariścandra's sacrifice.
Vasiṣṭha praises his patron Hariścandra and stakes ascetic merit upon the king's truthfulness.

Vatsara.note: Vatsara is Dhruva’s son by Bhramī.

Vicitravīrya.note: Vicitravīrya is Bhīṣma’s younger half-brother through Śantanu.
Bhīṣma abducts three princesses to obtain wives for Vicitravīrya.

Vidura.note: Vidura’s coded warning and escape plan help save Bhīma and his family.
Bhīṣma and Vidura serve together as guardians and counsellors of the Kurus.
Vidura warns against Duryodhana, opposes the dice scheme, and counsels peace.
Vidura secretly warns the Pāṇḍavas, frustrating Duryodhana’s murder plot.
Vidura joins Gandhari in warning the court against Duryodhana's destructive course.
He accompanies Gandhari and the elder household during their postwar withdrawal.
Vidura warns Yudhiṣṭhira about the incendiary plot and enables the escape.
Vidura repeatedly advises Yudhiṣṭhira and condemns the dice disaster.
Vidura mystically transfers or merges his life-force into Yudhiṣṭhira.

Vikarna.note: He defends her legal objection before Karṇa rejects his argument.

Vikarna.myth: Vikarna objects during the dice-hall outrage
Vikarna.note: Vikarna challenges Draupadī’s enslavement while Duryodhana’s faction continues the abuse.
Vikarna is one of Gandhari's sons.
She praises and mourns Vikarna after Bhīma kills him.
Vikarna disputes Draupadī's enslavement while Yudhiṣṭhira remains legally compromised.

Virāṭa.note: Virāṭa gives Uttarā to Abhimanyu, sealing a Matsya-Pāṇḍava alliance.
Arjuna serves in Virāṭa’s court while disguised as Bṛhannalā.
Virāṭa becomes Arjuna’s ally after the incognito year.
Disguised as Ballava, Bhīma serves Virāṭa as cook and court wrestler.
Drona participates in the Kuru raid upon Virāṭa’s cattle.
Drona kills Virāṭa during the Kurukṣetra war.
Disguised as Kanka, Yudhiṣṭhira serves Virāṭa as courtier and dice-player.
Virāṭa strikes the disguised Yudhiṣṭhira during a dice game and later apologizes.
After Yudhiṣṭhira reveals himself, Virāṭa becomes his ally.

Viśravas.note: Vibhishana is the son of the sage Viśravas.

Viśvedevas.note: The Viśvedevas are drawn into the narrative frame surrounding Hariścandra's intervention and Viśvāmitra's curse.

Viśvāmitra.note: Viśvāmitra serves among the ritual priests in versions of the Śunaḥśepa sacrifice.
Viśvāmitra wagers with Vasiṣṭha that he can expose or defeat Hariścandra's celebrated truthfulness.
Viśvāmitra takes Hariścandra's kingdom, demands further payment, and drives the sale of his family and self.

Viṣṇu.note: Dhruva worships and meditates upon Viṣṇu through austerity and mantra.
Viṣṇu gives Dhruva inspired speech and an imperishable celestial station.
Drona fixes his mind upon the supreme indestructible deity while entering yoga.
Hariścandra meditates upon the formless Viṣṇu or Brahman at the culmination of his ordeal.
Some modern retellings make Viṣṇu appear personally to end Hariścandra's ordeal.
Viṣṇu protects Prahlāda from weapons, poison, beasts, fire, water, and burial.
Viṣṇu bestows sovereignty and, in some accounts, eventual liberation.
Through Rāma’s developing identification with Viṣṇu, Sugrīva’s alliance enters a divine plan.

Vyāsa.note: Vyāsa explains that Arjuna’s divine power and allotted cosmic period have ended.
Vyāsa intervenes, orders surrender of the jewel, and confirms Kṛṣṇa’s sentence.
Aśvatthāman submits to Vyāsa before surrendering his jewel and departing.
The dynastic sage advises Bhīma and the other Pāṇḍavas.
Vyāsa engenders Kuru heirs after Bhīṣma refuses, and later counsels beside him.
He reveals former and divine causes that legitimize her polyandrous marriage.
Vyāsa is Duryodhana’s paternal grandfather through Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Vyāsa divides Gāndhārī’s flesh mass and oversees gestation in jars.
She hospitably serves Vyāsa when he arrives hungry and exhausted.

Vyāsa.myth: Vyāsa's boon of one hundred sons
Vyāsa.note: Pleased by her hospitality, Vyāsa grants her requested hundred sons.
Vyāsa prevents her discarding the fetal mass, divides it, and supervises incubation in jars.
Vyāsa grants Gandhari supernatural sight through her blindfold.
Vyāsa warns her against cursing the victorious Pāṇḍavas.
Vyāsa is Yudhiṣṭhira's grandfather in the Kuru genealogy.
Vyāsa advises him, defends Draupadī's marriage, teaches lore, and directs postwar restoration.

Vāli.myth: The two challenges and fraternal duels
Vāli.note: Sugrīva challenges Vāli twice; Rāma kills Vāli during the second duel.
Vāli beats and banishes Sugrīva, believing he deliberately usurped the throne.

Vāmadeva.note: Vāmadeva participates in the debate following the release of Hariścandra's substitute victim.

Vṛddhakṣatra.note: Arjuna’s arrow drops Jayadratha’s head into his father’s lap, fulfilling a curse.

Vṛṣaketu.note: Vṛṣaketu is Karṇa’s son, prominent chiefly in supplementary and regional traditions.

Vṛṣasena.note: Vṛṣasena is Karṇa’s son and battlefield comrade.

Yakṣas.note: Dhruva attacks Alakā and indiscriminately kills Yakṣas after Uttama’s death.
Dhruva ends hostilities and is reconciled with the Yakṣas’ lord Kubera.

Yama.note: Yama is associated with celestial weapons granted during Arjuna’s ascent.

Yama.myth: Infernal authority in the cremation-ground dream
Yama.note: Yama's messengers and infernal authority appear within Hariścandra's dream of punishment and rebirth.
Regional tellings sometimes replace Dharma with Yama as Hariścandra's disguised caṇḍāla master.
Nala carries Yama's marriage proposal to Damayantī.
Yama assumes Nala's form while competing for Damayantī.
Yama accepts Damayantī's choice and grants Nala excellence in dharma and food.
Yama extracts and binds Satyavān’s soul and carries it southward.
Sāvitrī follows Yama and wins successive concessions through dharmic argument.
Yama grants Sāvitrī five boons restoring both families’ fortunes and posterity.
Yama releases Satyavān’s soul and restores his life after Sāvitrī’s appeal.

Yaudheya.note: Yaudheya is Yudhiṣṭhira's son by Devikā.

Yuyutsu.note: Yuyutsu abandons Duryodhana’s side and joins the Pāṇḍavas before battle.
Yuyutsu defects from the Kauravas to Yudhiṣṭhira's side.
Yudhiṣṭhira gives Yuyutsu administrative responsibility during the succession.

Yādavas.note: She curses Kṛṣṇa's relatives to kill one another after thirty-six years.

Yāma deities.note: The Yāmas participate in the unsuccessful attempt to disrupt Dhruva.

the Aśvins.note: Nakula and Sahadeva's divine fathers appear with Yudhiṣṭhira in heaven.

the Cedis.note: Drona fights Cedi warriors during his battlefield command.

the Kekaya brothers.note: The Kekaya brothers are named among Drona’s opposing warriors.

Āyuṣmant.note: Āyuṣmant is Dhruva’s brother in a Purāṇic genealogical variant.

Āyuṣmān.note: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa names Āyuṣmān among Prahlāda’s sons.

Śabarī.myth: Variant direction of Rāma toward Sugrīva
Śabarī.note: Some later traditions have Śabarī redirect Rāma toward Sugrīva; no personal encounter is secure.

Śacī.note: Some northern and post-epic systems identify Draupadī with Indra's goddess-consort.

Śailūṣa.note: The gandharva Śailūṣa is Vibhishana’s father-in-law through Saramā.

Śaivyā.note: Śaivyā is Hariścandra's queen in Sanskrit ordeal narratives, with regional names Tārāmatī and Candramatī.
Hariścandra reluctantly sells his wife into domestic servitude to satisfy Viśvāmitra's demanded fee.

Śaivyā.myth: Recognition and attempted death on son's pyre
Śaivyā.note: The estranged spouses recognize each other and resolve to die together upon their son's pyre.
She is Satyavān’s mother; the personal name Śaivyā occurs only in some recensions.

Śakuni.note: Śakuni belongs to the hostile coalition, and Abhimanyu kills one of his brothers.
Bhāsa depicts Śakuni celebrating Abhimanyu’s unlawful killing.
Arjuna fights the cause supported by the architect of the dice fraud.
Bhīma threatens the dice-game antagonist and later fights against his faction.
His maternal uncle serves as political counsellor and close ally.

Śakuni.myth: Dice games at the Kuru court
Śakuni.note: Śakuni proposes the scheme and throws the dice on Duryodhana’s behalf.
Śakuni is Gandhari's brother and escorts her to her marriage.
She urges Duryodhana to cast off Śakuni's destructive advice.
Modern narratives make Śakuni a target of his magical deception and humiliation.
Śakuni serves as Yudhiṣṭhira's direct dice opponent and defeats him twice.

Śalya.note: Śalya fights Abhimanyu, whose attacks also kill Śalya’s son Rukmaratha.
Arjuna confronts Karṇa while Śalya serves as Karṇa’s reluctant charioteer.
Bhīma combats Śalya during the war.
Duryodhana secretly provides lavish hospitality, inducing Śalya to grant him a boon.
Śalya becomes Karṇa’s charioteer and later Duryodhana’s final army commander.
Śalya unwillingly drives Karṇa’s chariot while insulting and discouraging him.
Yudhiṣṭhira fights Śalya after preparing strategically for their confrontation.
Yudhiṣṭhira kills Śalya with a divinely potent spear.

Śani.note: Later Thirunallar tradition associates Nala with suffering and relief from Śani's affliction.

Śantanu.note: Bhīṣma renounces succession, marriage, and children so Śantanu may marry Satyavatī.

Śantanu.myth: Śantanu grants death at Bhīṣma’s choosing
Śantanu.note: Śantanu rewards Bhīṣma’s vow with control over the time of death.

Śarabha.note: Śarabha gives his opinion when Rāma’s allies debate admitting Vibhishana.

Śatarūpā.note: Dhruva is Śatarūpā’s grandson in the narrative genealogy.
Śatarūpā accompanies the royal party that welcomes Dhruva home.

Śatānīka.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Śatānīka.note: Śatānīka strikes him with a chariot wheel before being beheaded.
Her son by Nakula, later killed in the night raid.

Śaśirekhā.note: South Indian romance makes Śaśirekhā Abhimanyu’s beloved and wife.
He rescues or conceals her so she can marry Abhimanyu.
He assumes her appearance to deceive and humiliate the rival wedding party.

Śaṇḍa.note: Śaṇḍa attempts to instruct Prahlāda in Daitya statecraft.

Śibi.note: Some conflicting genealogical lists identify Śibi as Prahlāda’s brother.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa alternatively names Śibi as Prahlāda’s son.

Śikhaṇḍin.note: Śikhaṇḍin provides the shield and pretext enabling Arjuna to fell Bhīṣma.

Śikhaṇḍin.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Śikhaṇḍin.note: Aśvatthāman cuts down Śikhaṇḍin during the nocturnal massacre.
Bhīma and Śikhaṇḍin fight on the allied Pāṇḍava side against Bhīṣma.
Śikhaṇḍin shoots at Bhīṣma, who refuses to retaliate because of Śikhaṇḍin’s former sex.
Both are children of Drupada and allied within the Pāṇḍava cause.
Śikhaṇḍin serves in Yudhiṣṭhira's army and is deployed against Bhīṣma.

Śiva.note: Śiva indirectly enables Abhimanyu’s isolation by empowering Jayadratha to check the Pāṇḍavas.
Arjuna duels Śiva disguised as a hunter and is defeated.
After revealing himself, Śiva grants Arjuna the Pāśupata weapon.
In Himalayan pilgrimage legend, Bhīma grapples with Śiva disguised as a bull.
A figure named Śiva is Dhruva’s brother in the Harivaṃśa genealogy.
Śiva grants her repeatedly requested boon, producing her five-husband destiny.
The disputed local deity once called Duryodhana is increasingly identified as Someshvara, a form of Śiva.
Śiva.source: Sax, Himalayan fieldwork and cult testimony

Śiva.myth: Śiva's boon of one hundred sons
Śiva.note: Gandhari worships Śiva and receives his promise of one hundred sons.
Some later theatre and film endings make Śiva appear among those ending Hariścandra's ordeal.
Śiva appears among the gods following Narasiṃha’s victory.
Yudhiṣṭhira hears extensive Śiva theology and hymns from Bhīṣma and Kṛṣṇa.

Śiśumāra Prajāpati.note: Śiśumāra Prajāpati is Dhruva’s father-in-law through Bhramī.

Śiśupāla.note: Śiśupāla condemns the Jarāsandha killing and insults Bhīma and Kṛṣṇa.
Śiśupāla pursues or opposes the abduction while Karṇa fights for Duryodhana.
Śiśupāla challenges Yudhiṣṭhira's first honor for Kṛṣṇa and is killed there.

Śrutakarman.note: Śrutakarman is Arjuna’s son by Draupadī.

Śrutakarman.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Śrutakarman.note: Śrutakarman strikes Aśvatthāman and dies from his sword blow.
Her son by Arjuna; his name varies in the textual tradition.

Śrutakīrti.myth: Night raid on the Pāṇḍava camp
Śrutakīrti.note: Śrutakīrti shoots at Aśvatthāman and is beheaded by him.

Śrutasena.note: Her son by Sahadeva, later killed in the night raid.

Śrutāyus.note: Yudhiṣṭhira fights the named warrior Śrutāyus in the war catalogues.

Śrī.note: Draupadī is identified as a portion or manifestation of royal Fortune.

Śuka.note: Vibhishana detects or identifies Śuka while he spies in Rāma’s camp.

Śukra.note: Expanded later accounts list Śukra among Bhīṣma’s teachers.
Śukra is said to circumambulate Dhruva’s imperishable station.

Śunaḥśepa.note: Hariścandra accepts the purchased Śunaḥśepa, who is bound for sacrifice before hymns secure his release.

Śālva.note: Bhīṣma defeats Śālva while carrying away the three princesses.
Bhīṣma sends Ambā to Śālva, who rejects her after his defeat.

Śāradvat.note: Śāradvat is Aśvatthāman’s maternal ancestor through Kṛpī.

Śūrpaṇakhā.note: Śūrpaṇakhā is Vibhishana’s full sister in Vālmīki’s later genealogy.
Śūrpaṇakhā is his maternal half-sister in the competing Mahābhārata genealogy.

Ṛkṣarajas.note: Ṛkṣarajas is Sugrīva’s social or dynastic father.
